theme: The Branch of the LORD; the vineyard song
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 4:1-5:30. A beautiful promise of the Branch of the LORD is followed by the famous song of the vineyard. Read the song as a story, and notice how the listeners are caught by it.
settingTheScene: Chapter 4 closes the first section of Isaiah with a picture of a cleansed Jerusalem after judgment. Chapter 5 opens with a love song that suddenly turns into a lawsuit. Isaiah probably sang or recited it publicly at a feast. The vineyard, a common image for Israel, appears again and again in Scripture, in the Psalms (like Psalm 80, in two days), and in Jesus’ parables.
observation: “In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious” (4:2).
“And he who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy” (4:3).
“Then the LORD will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day, and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night” (4:5).
“Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard” (5:1).
“He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines” (5:2).
“What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it? When I looked for it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes?” (5:4).
“He looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry!” (5:7).
“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness” (5:20).
interpretation:
Chapter 4 begins with a bleak scene: seven women clinging to one man because the men have died in war. It shows the depth of the coming loss. Then comes the promise. “The branch of the LORD” will be beautiful and glorious. The word “branch” (Hebrew tsemach) is a title that will later become a name for the Messiah (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8). The survivors of Zion will be called holy. God will wash away the filth and cleanse the bloodstains. And he will cover the city with a canopy of cloud and fire, just as he did in the wilderness. After judgment, a new exodus.

Chapter 5 is a masterpiece of rhetoric. Isaiah sings of a friend who owned a vineyard on a fertile hill. He dug, cleared, planted choice vines, built a watchtower and a winepress. Everything necessary was done. And the vineyard produced wild grapes, sour and useless. The listeners must have enjoyed the song and probably sided with the owner. Then Isaiah turns the question on them: “What more was there to do?” The listeners are the vineyard. God looked for justice, and found bloodshed. He looked for righteousness and heard the cry of the oppressed.

The consequences are given: God will remove the hedge, break down the wall, and let it be trampled. The judgment is the withdrawal of protection. The following six woes detail the sins: greedy land accumulation, drunken feasting, mocking God’s plan, calling evil good, pride in one’s own wisdom, and bribery. Verse 20 is among the most relevant in the whole book. When a society reverses its moral categories, it is ripe for judgment.

The passage ends with the sound of a distant army. God whistles for Assyria from the ends of the earth. It is a dark picture. But the reader knows from chapter 4 that this is not the last word. The Branch will come.
connection: Jesus told his own vineyard parable of the wicked tenants who killed the owner’s son (Mark 12:1-12), clearly echoing Isaiah 5. In John 15:1-8 he says, “I am the true vine,” the faithful Israel who bears fruit. Jeremiah 23:5 and Zechariah 6:12 call the Messiah the Branch. Galatians 5:22-23 describes the fruit of the Spirit, the good grapes that God wants.
application:
Ask what kind of fruit your life is bearing. Is it justice, mercy, and righteousness, or sour grapes?

Notice where our culture calls evil good and good evil. Pray for clarity and courage.

Thank God for the Branch, Jesus, who is the true vine, and ask to abide in him.
prayerPrompts: Confess the wild grapes you have produced.
Ask Jesus, the true vine, to help you abide and bear fruit.
Thank God for all he has done for his vineyard.
